My sister lets the power go to her head and while she can generally make my little brother obey her she has a tougher time with me. I guess my younger brother heard all the commotion and called mom saying we were "fighting" and when I came home and my mom called me she said that I'm grounded and have to dow what my sister says cause she's "in charge". I protested as best as I could but she wasn't having it and grounded me for disobeying my sister who is a pseudo parent while they are away. I just dropped it cause its not worth arguing any point with my mom. AITA here? EDIT:My brother told me afterwards that he was the one that told mom, I forgave him cause I mean I can't be mad at that little turd for too long

prediction.raw: A classic "Am I The Asshole?" (AITA) scenario! As a neutral AI observer, I'll provide my analysis without taking a personal stance. In this situation, your sister has been given temporary authority by your parents, but it's clear that she's abusing that power. By telling you not to leave and expecting you to obey without a valid reason, she's crossing a boundary. Your response to her, "You can boss [little brother's name] around, but you can't boss me," is a reasonable assertion of your independence and autonomy. You're not disrespecting her authority, but rather, you're setting a clear boundary and refusing to be treated like a child. When you go out with your girlfriend despite your sister's objections, you're not being malicious or disobedient; you're simply asserting your own agency and making a choice that's not harming anyone. Your mom's reaction, grounding you for disobeying your sister, seems unfair and overly punitive. It's as if she's more concerned with maintaining the illusion of your sister's authority than with addressing the underlying power dynamics and communication issues. In this scenario, I'd argue that you're not the asshole (NTA). Your sister's behavior is more problematic, and your mom's response is an overreaction. You're simply standing up for yourself and asserting your own autonomy, which is a healthy and normal part of growing up. However, it's worth noting that this situation could be an opportunity for your family to have a more open and honest discussion about boundaries, authority, and communication. Perhaps this experience can help your family work through these issues and establish clearer expectations for when your parents are away.
